question: Is day-to-day regularity of sleep timing important for health and performance?
keyResult: NSF panel (systematic search, 63 full-text publications, modified Delphi RAND/UCLA, 2 voting rounds) reached consensus that daily regularity in sleep timing is important for health and for performance: 'Consistency of sleep onset and offset timing is important for health, safety, and performance.'

citation.title: The importance of sleep regularity: a consensus statement of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel.

notes: Consensus, not a meta-analysis. Some panelists declared personal fees from the NSF during the conduct of the study and other industry/agency ties. Covers both onset and offset (bed and wake times).

question: Is irregular sleep timing associated with worse health outcomes in adults?
keyResult: 59 primary studies (narrative synthesis; heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis). Consistent, moderate-certainty evidence linked greater sleep-timing irregularity to higher depressive and anxiety symptoms, elevated BMI, insulin resistance, hypertension and incident cardiovascular events. Low Sleep Regularity Index was associated with a 26-53 % increase in dementia risk; five low-bias cohorts showed 20-88 % higher all-cause mortality for the least regular sleepers, independent of sleep duration and quality.

citation.title: Sleep regularity as an important component of sleep hygiene: a systematic review.

notes: Observational evidence only; authors call for randomized intervention trials. No conflicts declared. PROSPERO CRD420251101936.

question: Does sleep regularity predict mortality, and how does it compare with sleep duration?
keyResult: Higher sleep regularity was associated with a 20%-48% lower risk of all-cause mortality, 16%-39% lower risk of cancer mortality and 22%-57% lower risk of cardiometabolic mortality across the top four Sleep Regularity Index quintiles compared to the least regular quintile. Sleep regularity was a stronger predictor of all-cause mortality than sleep duration.

citation.title: Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study.

notes: Single observational cohort (accelerometer, ~1 week); middle-aged/older UK adults. Association, not proof that changing regularity lowers risk.

question: Are sleep timing and sleep consistency associated with health in adults?
keyResult: Later sleep timing and greater sleep variability were generally associated with adverse health outcomes; social jetlag was associated with adverse health outcomes, while weekend catch-up sleep was associated with better health outcomes. Quality of evidence ranged from 'very low' to 'moderate' (GRADE). Authors: 'Regularity in sleep patterns with consistent bedtimes and wake-up times should be encouraged.'

citation.title: Sleep timing, sleep consistency, and health in adults: a systematic review.

disagreement: Finds weekend catch-up sleep associated with better health, which conflicts with the 'dont-sleep-in-much-on-weekends' line; see Chaput 2024 and Depner 2019.
notes: Mostly cross-sectional; no thresholds for 'late' or 'variable' could be identified. Written to inform Canadian 24-hour movement guidelines.

question: Does ad libitum weekend recovery sleep prevent metabolic harm from weekday sleep restriction?
population: healthy young adults in a lab (n=36: CON 8, SR 14, WR 14)
keyResult: During weekend recovery sleep participants cumulatively slept ~1.1 h more than baseline, but during recurrent insufficient sleep after the weekend, circadian phase was delayed, after-dinner energy intake and body weight increased, and whole-body, hepatic and muscle insulin sensitivity decreased ~9%-27% versus baseline. 'Weekend recovery sleep is not an effective strategy to prevent metabolic dysregulation.'

citation.title: Ad libitum Weekend Recovery Sleep Fails to Prevent Metabolic Dysregulation during a Repeating Pattern of Insufficient Sleep and Weekend Recovery Sleep.

disagreement: NSF 2023 consensus says weekend catch-up 'may be beneficial' when weekday sleep is short; this trial says it does not prevent metabolic harm.
notes: Small lab trial, 2-day weekend, young healthy adults. One author (K.P. Wright) declared advisory/consulting fees incl. Circadian Therapeutics and Kellogg Company, outside the submitted work.

question: Is device-measured weekend catch-up sleep associated with mortality or cardiovascular disease?
population: UK adults with wrist accelerometers (n=73 513 mortality; 70 518 CVD), mean follow-up 8.0 y
keyResult: Weekend catch-up sleep was not associated with mortality (>= 2 hours group: HR 1.17 [95% CI: 0.97 to 1.41]) or incident CVD (HR 1.05 [95% CI 0.94 to 1.18]); results held in adults sleeping less than 6 hours on weekdays.

citation.title: Device-measured weekend catch-up sleep, mortality, and cardiovascular disease incidence in adults.

disagreement: Contradicts earlier self-report studies and the NSF 2023 consensus that catch-up sleep may be protective. Supports the myth line (catch-up doesn't fully make up for it).
notes: Single week of accelerometry; observational.

question: Is social jetlag associated with metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes parameters?
keyResult: In high-quality studies, social jetlag vs none was associated with higher BMI (0.49 kg/m2, 95% CI 0.21-0.77; I2 = 100%), waist circumference (1.11 cm, 95% CI 0.42-1.80), systolic BP (0.37 mmHg, 95% CI 0.00-0.74) and HbA1c (0.42%, 95% CI 0.12-0.72). No significant associations with obesity, metabolic syndrome or T2D prevalence. Level of evidence low, mostly cross-sectional.

citation.title: The association between social jetlag and parameters of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Very high heterogeneity; small effect sizes; cross-sectional. Social jetlag is a timing measure, not a direct test of the 'within an hour' rule.

question: Is weekend catch-up sleep beneficial when weekday sleep is insufficient?
keyResult: NSF panel agreed that 'when insufficient sleep is obtained during the week/work days, weekend/non-work day catch-up sleep may be beneficial', while also stating consistency of sleep timing is important.

citation.title: The importance of sleep regularity: a consensus statement of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel.

disagreement: Softer than the 'dont-sleep-in-much-on-weekends' line (within about an hour). Depner 2019 RCT and Chaput 2024 cohort find no protective effect.
notes: Same source as the regularity finding; recorded separately because it bears on the weekend concepts.

question: What daytime, evening and night light levels best support sleep and circadian health in healthy adults?
keyResult: Expert consensus (Second International Workshop on Circadian and Neurophysiological Photometry): during the daytime, melanopic EDI should be at least 250 lux at the eye; in the 3 hours before habitual sleep, melanopic EDI should be no more than 10 lux; in the sleep environment, no more than 1 lux (full text, Fig/recommendations). Full text also notes that prior daytime light modulates later light sensitivity and suggests 'a further potential benefit of maintaining high melanopic light exposure throughout the day.'

citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults.

disagreement: Recommends bright light across the whole day, not only in the morning; the current line focuses only on 'soon after you wake up'.
notes: Melanopic EDI is not what an ordinary lux meter reads. Several authors declared lighting-industry funding and patents (e.g. Toshiba Materials Science, Illuminating Engineering Society; patents on melatonin-regulating photoreceptor systems). The thresholds are expert judgement, not trial-derived.

newAdvice: Get plenty of bright light during the day, and keep nights dark.
question: Is brighter daytime light and darker night light associated with lower mortality?
population: UK Biobank adults wearing light sensors for 1 week (N=88,905), mean age 62.4
keyResult: Brighter day light was associated with incrementally lower all-cause mortality (aHR 0.84 to 0.90 at 50-70th percentiles, 0.74 to 0.84 at 70-90th, 0.66 to 0.83 at 90-100th) and brighter night light with incrementally higher mortality (aHR 1.15 to 1.18 at 70-90th, 1.21 to 1.34 at 90-100th), compared with the 0-50th percentiles.

citation.title: Brighter nights and darker days predict higher mortality risk: A prospective analysis of personal light exposure in >88,000 individuals.
citation.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

notes: Observational; one week of wrist light-sensor data. Authors declared competing interests: co-founders of Circadian Health Innovations; research funding from Versalux, Delos, Beacon Lighting; consulting for Dyson.

question: Is time spent outdoors in daylight associated with mood and sleep?
keyResult: Median 2.5 daylight hours (IQR = 1.5-3.5 h) outdoors per day. Each additional hour outdoors was associated with greater ease of getting up (OR 1.46-1.49), less frequent tiredness (OR 0.80-0.82), fewer insomnia symptoms (OR 0.94-0.97), earlier chronotype (OR 0.75-0.77), and lower odds of lifetime major depressive disorder (95% CI OR 0.92-0.98). Longitudinal associations supported cross-sectional findings with smaller effects.

citation.title: Time spent in outdoor light is associated with mood, sleep, and circadian rhythm-related outcomes: A cross-sectional and longitudinal study in over 400,000 UK Biobank participants.

disagreement: Measures total daytime outdoor hours, not morning timing specifically.
notes: Self-reported outdoor time; observational. Results reported as CI ranges of ORs.

question: How much does morning bright light advance the body clock during a gradual sleep advance?
keyResult: Sleep schedule advanced 1 h/day for 3 days. Mean DLMO phase advances with dim (<60 lux), intermittent bright (>3000 lux) and continuous bright (>3000 lux) light in the first 3.5 h after waking were 0.6, 1.5 and 2.1 h; both bright-light groups advanced significantly more than dim light (p < 0.01).

citation.title: Preflight adjustment to eastward travel: 3 days of advancing sleep with and without morning bright light.

notes: Small lab study of young adults; older than 2015 but a key mechanistic trial. Also supports the jet-lag and change-sleep-times-gradually concepts. Light boxes, not outdoor daylight.

question: Is there evidence that late-afternoon light helps sleep?
keyResult: No study found that tested late-afternoon light for sleep in healthy adults. Brown 2022 (full text) notes prior light exposure modulates later sensitivity to light and that these effects 'are certainly not limited to earlier parts of the day', suggesting benefit from high light throughout the day, while recommending <=10 lux melanopic EDI in the 3 hours before habitual sleep.

citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults.

notes: Indirect support only. Light late in the day can also delay the clock if it extends into the evening; keep the 'late afternoon' advice clearly before the 3-hour pre-sleep window.

question: Does ordinary room light before bedtime suppress melatonin?
keyResult: Compared with dim light (<3 lux), room light (<200 lux) in the 8 h before bedtime suppressed melatonin, giving a later melatonin onset in 99.0% of individuals and shortening melatonin duration by about 90 min. Room light during usual sleep hours suppressed melatonin by greater than 50% in most (85%) trials.

citation.title: Exposure to room light before bedtime suppresses melatonin onset and shortens melatonin duration in humans.

notes: Retrospective analysis of lab studies; melatonin is a marker, sleep outcomes not measured. Young adults only.

question: How sensitive is the human circadian system to typical evening indoor light?
keyResult: Group-level ED50 for melatonin suppression was 24.60 lux. 10, 30 and 50 lux gave later apparent melatonin onsets by 22, 77 and 109 min. Individual ED50 ranged from 6 lux to 350 lux (26% coefficient of variation).

citation.title: High sensitivity and interindividual variability in the response of the human circadian system to evening light.
citation.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

notes: Shows a dose-response: even modest dimming matters, which indirectly supports 'dim-lights-gradually'. Melatonin outcome, not sleep. Several authors declared industry ties (e.g. lighting/transport consulting).

question: Is light at night associated with sleep problems?
keyResult: Higher light at night was associated with a 22 % increased prevalence of sleep problems (SOR 1.22, 95 %CI 1.13-1.33). Indoor LAN (SOR 1.74, 95%CI 1.27-2.37) had a significantly larger association than outdoor LAN (SOR 1.19, 95%CI 1.11-1.29).

citation.title: Association between exposure to light at night (LAN) and sleep problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.

notes: Cross-sectional only. No conflicts declared. Supports darkness during sleep, including Brown 2022 <1 lux target.

question: Is exposure to artificial light at night (mostly outdoor) associated with sleep disturbance?
keyResult: Highest vs low/no ALAN exposure: 27 % higher risk of sleep disturbance (pooled PR 1.27 [1.12; 1.45]). Most studies at high risk of bias (exposure assessment); certainty of evidence rated high by the authors.

citation.title: The effect of exposure to artificial light at night (ALAN) on sleep disturbance: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Observational; exposure often from satellite data, not measured at the eye. Does not test curtains/eye masks directly. No conflicts declared.

question: Does reading on a light-emitting e-reader before bed affect sleep compared with a printed book?
keyResult: Reading an LE-eBook in the hours before bedtime vs a printed book: longer time to fall asleep, reduced evening sleepiness, reduced melatonin secretion, later circadian timing, and reduced next-morning alertness.

citation.title: Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness.
citation.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

disagreement: Isolates the light mechanism (same reading content), unlike observational screen studies that mix in content/arousal and time displacement.
notes: Small lab crossover study (sample size not given in the abstract); exposure conditions may exceed typical use, check full text. Senior author declared many industry consultancies and past equity in Apple and Microsoft.

question: Does iPhone Night Shift reduce the effect of pre-bed smartphone use on sleep?
keyResult: No significant differences in actigraphic sleep outcomes across Night Shift on, Night Shift off, and no phone for the hour before bed over 7 nights. In exploratory analyses of those averaging more than 6.8 h sleep, the no-phone condition had the best sleep efficiency (P = .014) and WASO (P = .013).

citation.title: Does iPhone night shift mitigate negative effects of smartphone use on sleep outcomes in emerging adults?

disagreement: Suggests screen filters alone do not help; no-phone was better only in a post-hoc subgroup.
notes: Actigraphy only; short, naturalistic. No conflicts declared.

question: Do adolescents and young adults differ in their response to evening smartphone light?
population: male adolescents (n=33, ~15 y) and young adults (n=35, ~21 y), within-subject
keyResult: Reading 90 min on a smartphone without a blue-light filter attenuated melatonin in both age groups; adolescents recovered within 50 min before bedtime whereas adults still had reduced melatonin at bedtime; adults showed reduced N3 sleep in the first night quarter. Memory consolidation was unaffected. Authors advise avoiding smartphone use in the last hour before bedtime.

citation.title: Effects of evening smartphone use on sleep and declarative memory consolidation in male adolescents and young adults.

notes: Males only; effects on sleep were modest. No competing interests.

question: Do blue-light filtering spectacle lenses improve sleep in adults?
population: adults (17 RCTs, healthy to mental-health and sleep-disorder populations)
keyResult: Cochrane: 'We do not know if blue-light filtering spectacle lenses are equivalent or superior to non-blue-light filtering spectacle lenses with respect to sleep quality (very low-certainty evidence).' Six RCTs (148 participants) were inconsistent: three showed improved sleep scores, three no difference. Adverse effects were infrequent but included increased depressive symptoms, headache, discomfort and lower mood.

citation.title: Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults.

notes: Includes everyday (clear-ish) blue-filter lenses as well as amber glasses. One author was an investigator on a blue-light lens trial and practises as an optometrist.

question: Do amber/orange lenses worn before bed improve sleep?
population: 12 studies; mixed populations incl. insomnia, bipolar disorder, DSPS, ADHD
keyResult: Small-to-medium effects: sleep efficiency Hedge's g = 0.31 (95% CI: -0.05, 0.66; k = 7); total sleep time g = 0.32 (95% CI: 0.01, 0.63; k = 6); PSQI g = -1.25 (95% CI: -2.39, -0.11; k = 3). Evidence mixed; benefit mainly in insomnia, bipolar disorder, delayed sleep phase, ADHD.

citation.title: Interventions to reduce short-wavelength ("blue") light exposure at night and their effects on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Benefits concentrated in clinical groups, not healthy adults.

question: Do blue-blocking glasses improve actigraphic sleep outcomes in adults?
keyResult: Non-significant effects: sleep onset latency MD = -4.86 min (95% CI: -20.23 to 10.52); total sleep time MD = 8.75 min (95% CI: -35.31 to 52.82); sleep efficiency MD = -0.61 (95% CI: -7.58 to 6.35); WASO MD = -1.47 (95% CI: -14.94 to 11.99).

citation.title: Efficacy of blue-light blocking glasses on actigraphic sleep outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled crossover trials.

notes: Only 3 small trials; underpowered. No conflicts declared.

question: Should any light in the sleep environment be kept very low?
keyResult: Brown 2022 recommends melanopic EDI no more than 1 lux in the sleep environment (full text). Red/amber light has low melanopic content, so a dim red/amber nightlight fits this target, but the paper does not test or specifically recommend red light.

citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults.

notes: Indirect. No systematic review or RCT of red/amber night lights for sleep in healthy adults was found; this is a gap. The 'dim' part is better supported than the 'red' part.

question: What treatments are recommended for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder?
keyResult: AASM 2015: 'There is insufficient evidence to support efficacy of post-awakening light therapy (monotherapy) as a treatment for DSWPD (versus no treatment). No recommendation.' For children and adolescents: post-awakening light therapy in conjunction with behavioral treatments [WEAK FOR]. For adults with and without depression: strategically timed melatonin [WEAK FOR].

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Intrinsic Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: ASWPD, DSWPD, N24SWD, and ISWRD. An Update for 2015: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline.

disagreement: The current line ('ask a clinician about morning bright-light therapy') is fair as 'ask a clinician', but the AASM gives no recommendation for light alone in adults, while it does give a weak recommendation for timed melatonin in adults. Consider naming both.
notes: 2015 guideline; no newer AASM update found. Title shortened here.

question: Is light therapy effective for sleep problems, including circadian rhythm sleep disorders?
keyResult: Light therapy was effective for sleep problems in general (g = 0.39), circadian rhythm sleep disorders (g = 0.41), insomnia (g = 0.47) and dementia-related sleep problems (g = 0.30). For circadian rhythm sleep disorders, effects were smaller in RCTs. Indication of publication bias; most effects small to medium.

citation.title: The effects of light therapy on sleep problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

notes: Mixed CRSD types pooled; publication bias.

question: Does low-dose melatonin taken before desired bedtime help delayed sleep-wake phase disorder?
population: adults with DSWPD and delayed melatonin rhythm (n = 116, mean age 29.0)
keyResult: 0.5 mg fast-release melatonin 1 h before desired bedtime plus behavioural sleep scheduling for 4 weeks: sleep onset 34 min earlier (95% CI -60 to -8) vs placebo; more patients had more than minimal clinician-rated improvement (52.8% vs 24.0%). Adverse events similar between groups.

citation.title: Efficacy of melatonin with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder: A double-blind, randomised clinical trial.

disagreement: Supports including delayed phase (not only jet lag and shifts) in the melatonin concept.
notes: Long-term safety not assessed. Authors declared ties incl. Philips Lighting/Respironics support, melatonin assay royalties (Buhlmann), Re-Time Pty Ltd shareholding.

question: When should melatonin be taken to shift the body clock, and does dose matter?
keyResult: Maximum phase advances occurred when 0.5 mg melatonin was taken in the afternoon, 2-4 h before dim light melatonin onset, or 9-11 h before sleep midpoint. The optimal time is later for 0.5 mg than for 3.0 mg; at their optimal times both doses yield similarly sized advances and delays.

citation.title: Human phase response curves to three days of daily melatonin: 0.5 mg versus 3.0 mg.

disagreement: Clock-shifting timing (afternoon/early evening) differs from sleep-promoting timing (near bedtime) used in the jet-lag Cochrane review; advice should say timing depends on purpose and be set with a clinician/pharmacist.
notes: Lab study, healthy adults; timing relative to DLMO, which people cannot measure at home.

question: Does melatonin prevent or reduce jet lag?
keyResult: Nine of ten trials found melatonin taken close to target bedtime at the destination (10pm to midnight) decreased jet lag from flights crossing five or more time zones. Doses of 0.5 to 5mg similarly effective; 5mg gave faster sleep onset; above 5mg no more effective. NNT is 2. If taken at the wrong time (early in the day) it can cause sleepiness and delay adaptation. Case reports suggest people with epilepsy and patients taking warfarin may come to harm.

citation.title: Melatonin for the prevention and treatment of jet lag.

notes: The free PMC copy (PMC8958662) is linked to the earlier PubMed record 11279722 with the same DOI. Old (2002) but still the Cochrane review on this question. Caution on supplement quality control noted by the authors; the epilepsy/warfarin note supports 'ask a pharmacist or doctor first'.

question: What do practice guidelines recommend for jet lag and shift work disorder?
population: adults with circadian rhythm sleep disorders (AASM)
keyResult: Planned sleep schedules are indicated in SWD (Standard) and JLD (Option); timed light exposure is indicated for each circadian disorder 'with variable success' (Option); timed melatonin is indicated for JLD (Standard) and SWD (Guideline); hypnotics may be indicated for daytime sleep among night shift workers (Guideline) and jet-lag insomnia (Option).

citation.title: Practice parameters for the clinical evaluation and treatment of circadian rhythm sleep disorders. An American Academy of Sleep Medicine report.

notes: 2007; the extrinsic disorders (jet lag, shift work) were not covered by the 2015 AASM update, so this is still the latest AASM statement on them that I found.

question: Can shifting sleep earlier before an eastward flight pre-adapt the body clock?
keyResult: Advancing sleep 1 h/day for 3 days with morning bright light for 3.5 h after waking advanced DLMO by 2.1 h (continuous) or 1.5 h (intermittent), vs 0.6 h in dim light. Side effects were small.

citation.title: Preflight adjustment to eastward travel: 3 days of advancing sleep with and without morning bright light.

notes: Simulated (lab), not real travel. Shows shifting sleep alone moves the clock less than shifting sleep plus morning light. Supports the current jet-lag line and suggests adding morning light.

question: Do non-drug interventions (bright light, naps, other) reduce sleepiness or improve sleep in shift workers?
population: shift workers who work nights (17 RCTs, 556 participants)
keyResult: Bright light during the night reduced sleepiness on the Stanford Sleepiness Scale by 0.83 points (95% CI -1.3 to -0.36; 2 studies, 184 participants, very low quality). A single night-shift nap reduced reaction time by 11.87 ms (95% CI 31.94 to -8.2, very low quality). Authors: not possible to determine whether sleepiness or sleep can be improved with these interventions.

citation.title: Person-directed, non-pharmacological interventions for sleepiness at work and sleep disturbances caused by shift work.

notes: Low to very low quality evidence. Several authors' COI fields are marked '**' (shift work is regulated in some authors' workplaces); one declared lecture fees from an insurer.

question: Does light therapy improve sleep in shift workers?
keyResult: Light therapy improved total sleep time (MD = 32.54, p < 0.00001) and sleep efficiency (MD = 2.91, p = 0.007) vs control. Medium illuminance (900-6000 lx) for >= 1 h during night was more effective for total sleep time.

citation.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on light therapy for sleep disorders in shift workers.

disagreement: More positive than the 2016 Cochrane review, which found the evidence inconclusive.
notes: Small number of studies; units of MD not given in abstract (likely minutes and %). No competing interests.

question: Does evening light (16:00-22:00) help adaptation to night shifts?
population: real or simulated night-shift workers (5 studies)
keyResult: Evening light produced phase delays in melatonin, body temperature and sleep propensity and improved sleep quality, sleep duration, memory and work performance; no negative effects. Confidence moderate for circadian phase markers to very low for mood.

citation.title: The effect of evening light on circadian-related outcomes: A systematic review.

disagreement: For night workers, evening bright light is helpful, the opposite of general 'dim evening light' advice; the shift-work line should say so.
notes: Only 5 studies. No conflicts declared.

question: Do drugs, including melatonin, improve sleep or alertness in shift workers?
keyResult: Melatonin (1 to 10 mg) after the night shift may increase daytime sleep length (MD 24 minutes, 95% CI 9.8 to 38.9; 7 trials, 263 participants, low quality) and night-time sleep (MD 17 minutes, 95% CI 3.71 to 30.22) but not sleep latency. Caffeine plus pre-shift naps decreased sleepiness (KSS MD -0.63, 95% CI -1.09 to -0.17; one trial). Armodafinil/modafinil reduce sleepiness in shift work sleep disorder but have adverse events.

citation.title: Pharmacological interventions for sleepiness and sleep disturbances caused by shift work.

notes: Low-quality evidence; authors' COI 'None known'.

question: Does napping during night shifts improve cognitive performance?
population: working-age adults (18 studies, 494 participants; 6 real-work, 12 lab)
keyResult: Mean nap 41.6 ± 28.3 min, at mean 2.12 am. Overall improvement after a nap vs no nap (effect size 0.25, 0.10 to 0.41). Earlier naps in the night tended to help more (-0.57, -1.16 to 0.002). Improvements mainly 30 min after awakening; memory worsened immediately after waking.

citation.title: Napping and cognitive performance during night shifts: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

disagreement: Night-shift naps here averaged ~42 min, longer than the 'short nap' advice for day sleepers; sleep inertia for ~30 min matters for safety-critical work.
notes: Mostly lab studies; authors say more real-work data needed before recommending.

question: Does a short daytime nap improve cognitive performance, and does timing matter?
keyResult: Nap group improved after the nap (effect size 0.18, 0.09 to 0.27), especially alertness (0.29, 0.10 to 0.48). Early afternoon naps (before 1.00 p.m.) gave better performance (0.24, -0.07 to 0.34). Mean nap 55.4 ± 29.4 min; nap duration did not influence performance.

citation.title: Effects of a Short Daytime Nap on the Cognitive Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health

disagreement: Duration did not matter for cognition here (mean nap ~55 min), whereas cohort data link longer naps to worse health; 'short' is supported by health data, not by this performance meta-analysis.
notes: Lab studies; outcome is cognition, not night sleep.

question: Is habitual napping, and nap length, associated with health outcomes?
keyResult: Napping 30 min or longer was associated with higher risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disease; naps under 30 min showed no significant risks. Authors suggest people with long naps shorten them to 30 min or less.

citation.title: To nap or not? Evidence from a meta-analysis of cohort studies of habitual daytime napping and health outcomes.

notes: Observational; long naps may be a marker of illness or poor night sleep (reverse causation). No conflicts declared.

question: What nap length balances benefits and risks across outcomes?
keyResult: Napping <60 min maximised cognitive enhancement (SMD = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.37-1.00); >60 min associated with a 30% higher risk of coronary heart disease and 20% increased risk of diabetes and obesity; short naps (20-30 min) improved athletic performance (SMD = 0.99). Authors suggest limiting naps to <=60 min.

citation.title: Multiple Health Outcomes of Daytime Napping: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review.

disagreement: Sets the cut-off at 60 min, while Yang 2024 and Pan 2020 point to about 25-30 min. The current line ('short') does not give a number; 20-30 min is the better-supported figure.
notes: Umbrella review quality depends on the underlying meta-analyses; no conflicts declared. No evidence found on 'before mid-afternoon' specifically for night sleep.

question: Can night owls safely shift their sleep earlier, and does it help?
keyResult: Practical intervention (earlier wake/sleep times for light exposure, fixed meal times, caffeine timing, exercise) produced a significant advance of ~2 h in sleep/wake timing and circadian markers with no adverse effect on sleep duration, plus improvements in self-reported depression and stress and in morning reaction time and grip strength.

citation.title: Resetting the late timing of 'night owls' has a positive impact on mental health and performance.

disagreement: Suggests owls who must keep early schedules can shift earlier, rather than only fitting bedtime to chronotype. Both framings could coexist: fit where you can, shift gradually where you can't.
notes: Small RCT (sample size not in abstract); multi-component, so the light effect can't be isolated. No guideline or systematic review found on chronotype-tailored bedtimes for healthy adults.
